newsitem.title: UK: UK churches attack politicians for ignoring poor.
newsitem.headline: UK churches attack politicians for ignoring poor.

text.p: Britain's churches on Tuesday attacked politicians for using tax cuts for the middle classes as a vote winner, and called for higher taxes to create new jobs and narrow the social divide.
"In the British election campaign, the political parties are competing for votes by promising low taxation," said a report produced for the Council of Churches for Britain and Ireland.
"When so many are living in poverty and unemployment, it is wrong to give priority to the claims of those who are already well off."
The report, representing all Christian faiths, was seen as the hardest-hitting critique of social policy since 1985 when the Church of England highlighted poverty in Britain's cities.
Economist Andrew Britton, executive secretary to the report's working party, told a news conference: "Society should be prepared to meet higher taxes for the common good."
The result of 18 months of talks with politicians, trade unions, employers and the jobless, the report aims to alert public attention to poverty and high unemployment.
"We seem, in some parts of our islands, to be heading for a social crisis as mutual resentment between the haves and have-nots builds up," it concluded.

Church leaders denied it was an attack on any one political party but they admitted the timing of the report, four weeks before the May 1 election, was crucial, and defended the right of the church to intervene in politics.
"It's not an attack on any one position," said David Sheppard, Anglican Bishop of Liverpool.
"If there is a target at which the report aims it is the fatalism which wrings the hands and assumes that nothing can be done...It says that if we have the will we can change things."

Sheppard continued: "Elections are surely proper times to raise great questions of policy which affect so many people's lives...The churches' contact with all sections of society gives them both a close knowledge and a clear duty to examine these large questions."

The report claims government statistics understate the number of people out of work by as much as 50 percent, and says higher taxes could create new jobs in areas such as services and construction. As well as increasing public sector jobs, it proposes tax reforms to encourage more employment in the private sector.

"Compared with the rest of Europe, Britain has a relatively low ratio of taxation to GDP...it would be possible to add several percentage points of GDP to taxation in Britain over a run of years," it said.
However the report did not set out detailed proposals of the tax rises it advocates.

The opposition Labour Party praised the report which supports its policy of introducing a minimum wage and the European Social Chapter. But the ruling Conservatives said that while "the aims were laudable, its prescription is wrong in almost every respect."
